title: Ang 654–658: Sorath's Bhagats
tomorrow: what medicine does an old man ask for when his body gives out?

lines: YOU CAN'T LEAVE. I WON'T LET YOU.
cards: Some love songs are bold enough to make you blush: you can't leave, I won't let you.
On these pages of Sorath, the hymns belong to the bhagats, saints whose songs the Gurus set in the Granth: Kabir, Namdev, and Ravidas, whom tradition remembers as a leatherworker.
And Ravidas, answering yesterday's question, dares something close to that love song. He tells God: I've tied you up.

teach.h: I'M BOUND; I'VE BOUND YOU WITH LOVE.
teach.b: Here's Ravidas, in paraphrase. If I'm bound by the noose of attachment, then I have bound you with the bonds of love. Go on, try to free yourself.
I've been freed by worshiping you. Sikh readers hear that line in more than one way. Some hear daring intimacy.
Their best case: 'go on, try to free yourself' is a tease, and you only tease someone you're close to. Ravidas isn't keeping a respectful distance. He's so near that love itself becomes a rope.
Others hear humility first. Their best case is the opening: Ravidas admits he's the one tied up, by attachment.
His hold on God isn't strength; it's a beggar's grip.
And the freedom at the end comes from worship, not from out-binding anybody.
Both readings start from the same honesty: I'm bound. Where they part is in the tone of the second line, a lover's dare or a servant's clinging.
Kabir and Namdev sing on these pages too, and the Granth sets all their hymns among the Gurus' own, read and honored as the Guru's word.

how: Sikhs read the bhagats' hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib with the same reverence as the Gurus' own; in each raga they come after the Gurus' hymns, under each bhagat's name.

games.q: your friend says Ravidas's line is pure daring love. you hear humility. what's the best case for her side?

games.why: her strongest case is the tone of the second line: love close enough to tease. yours is the first line: he's the one bound, freed only by worship.

practice: Clasp your hands together loosely in your lap, the way you'd hold someone's hand on a long walk. Keep that grip for the sit, not tight, not letting go. Let the breath come and go through it.
